source: Bazazi et al. (2019) Self-serving incentives impair collective decisions by increasing conformity (PLoS ONE 14(11):e0224725)
finding: Seeing the group mean cut diversity and raised group error only when people were paid for their own accuracy. Paid for group accuracy, people stayed diverse and accurate.
numbers: 141 people in 23 groups of 4-8 (70 individual payoff, 71 collective payoff). Task: Where in London map estimates. Social info = star at group mean of Response 1. Diversity, individual payoff: 99.88% probability of less diversity with social info; collective payoff 73.35%. Group error, individual payoff: 99.57% probability of higher error with social info; collective 69.13%.
quote: knowledge about others' responses reduced the wisdom of the crowd and, crucially, this effect depended on how people were rewarded
limits: Small lab sample, one task, social info only as the mean (no individual answers, no confidence). Bayesian probability of direction, not frequentist tests. The overall payoff difference was weak (diversity 76.25%, error 65.35%); the effect lives in the interaction.
agent_relevance: Showing one attempt's answer to another attempt is the same as showing a self-interested estimator the group mean. Keep attempts blind to each other (G4/G9).

source: Bazazi et al. (2019) Self-serving incentives impair collective decisions by increasing conformity (PLoS ONE 14(11):e0224725) - restatement of Lorenz 2011
finding: Bazazi restates Lorenz 2011: group estimates were less accurate whenever people saw others' estimates or the average, yet confidence went up. Also notes that when people maximise their own accuracy, using social info helps them but hurts the group.
numbers: No new numbers in this passage. Theory side: relative-performance contests make people discount public signals; individual-accuracy payoffs make them use the public signal.
quote: although collective performance deteriorated when social information was presented, individuals exhibited more confidence
limits: Second-hand description of Lorenz.
agent_relevance: Confidence rising while group accuracy falls is the same trap as an agent trusting agreement among its own samples (G4).

source: Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer, Helbing (2011) How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect, PNAS 108(22)
finding: Founding result. Mild social influence shrinks the spread of guesses without improving the mean, and raises confidence.
numbers: From memory, NOT verified this session: about 144 students, 12 estimation questions, three information conditions (none, aggregated, full). Check against the paper before use.
limits: Could not open: pnas.org returned 403 and PMC returned a browser check. Only Bazazi's description was read.
agent_relevance: Origin of the pattern G4 guards against.

source: Becker, Centola, Brackbill (2017) Network dynamics of social influence in the wisdom of crowds, PNAS 114(26)
finding: Boundary condition on Lorenz. In decentralised networks, repeated social influence improved accuracy.
numbers: 1,360 online participants; 13 trials; networks of 40, plus 320 controls. Decentralised: SD of guesses fell 43% over 3 rounds, mean individual error -23%, group mean error 0.69 to 0.62 SD (-10%), median 0.76 to 0.67 (-12%). Control: SD -3%, no change in group mean.
limits: Figures come from a model-written summary of the PMC page. Gain depends on accurate people carrying more weight (revision coefficient rho=0.41).
agent_relevance: Influence helps only when weight tracks accuracy. A scaffold has no reliable accuracy signal for its own attempts, so isolation is the safe default.

source: Becker, Centola, Brackbill (2017) Network dynamics of social influence in the wisdom of crowds - centralised networks
finding: When one hub was highly connected, the group moved to the hub's first guess, for better or worse.
numbers: Hub's initial belief toward truth (12 trials): group mean error -43%, median -48%. Hub away from truth (13 trials): mean error +19%, median +32%. Correlation of hub's first guess with group shift rho=0.92 (n=57). Revision coefficient had no link to improvement (rho=-0.16).
limits: Same caveat as the previous line.
agent_relevance: One dominant attempt (a long, confident trace) acts like a hub and can drag everything else. Matches the SNLA result.

source: Kao, Berdahl, Couzin et al. (2018) Counteracting estimation bias and social influence to improve the wisdom of crowds, J R Soc Interface
finding: Guesses are lognormal: the mean overestimates and the median underestimates. A corrected mean stayed robust under social influence; the max-likelihood aggregator did not.
numbers: 812 new participants in 5 jar datasets (n=36, 51, 602, 69, 54; 54 to 27,852 objects). 602 people in the influence experiment: 231 ignored social info, 371 used it. Influence weight rose with displacement (0.65) and group size (0.37). Corrected measures beat standard in 58-78% of simulations. No hidden experts (p=0.938).
limits: Jelly-bean numerosity only. Summary of the page, not the full PDF.
agent_relevance: Pick an aggregator that is robust to shared bias when samples may be correlated.

source: Herd Behavior: Investigating Peer Influence in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (2025) - confidence
finding: LLM agents herd. They flip more when their own confidence is low and the peer looks confident. Following the most persuasive peer answer lowered factual accuracy.
numbers: Two-agent test with the 2nd-most-likely answer as peer answer: average flip rate 0.48. Benchmarks: MMLU-Pro (12,032 questions), GPQA-Diamond, ARC-Challenge, OpinionQA, GlobalOpinionQA, SOCIAL IQA. Models: OpenAI gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1 family. Peer persona: graduate degree 0.51, high school 0.46, employer 0.54 average flip rate.
limits: Multiple choice only. Peer answer chosen to be persuasive. Models all from one vendor.
agent_relevance: Any attempt that reads another's answer is exposed to this. Keep context fresh per attempt (G4).

source: Herd Behavior: Investigating Peer Influence in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (2025) - format and control
finding: Presentation format moves herding more than prompts do. Showing disagreeing peers first raised conformity. A 'be stubborn' or 'be agreeable' system prompt did almost nothing.
numbers: Five agents, 500 MMLU-Pro and 500 GlobalOpinionQA items filtered to max initial probability <0.8. Strong-factors bundle: flip rate 0.63 and 0.59, group accuracy 0.29 (MMLU-Pro). Weak-factors bundle: flip 0.36 and 0.23, entropy 0.28 and 0.22. Strong and weak prompt conditions both had flip rate 0.55, same as baseline.
limits: Group accuracy counts only unanimous correct answers, so it is harsh. Prompt control weak on MMLU-Pro, some effect on opinion items.
agent_relevance: Isolation by construction beats isolation by instruction. Telling a model to think for itself did not work.

source: Bertalanic & Fortuna (2026) The Cost of Consensus: Isolated Self-Correction Prevails Over Unguided Homogeneous Multi-Agent Debate - accuracy
finding: Same-model debate often did worse than one agent revising alone, at 2.1-3.4 times the tokens.
numbers: 10 agents, 3 rounds, GSM-Hard and MMLU-Hard, 7-8B models. Ministral-3-8B GSM-Hard: debate 20.7%, self-correction 48.3%, single shot 24.7% (p<0.001). Qwen2.5-7B MMLU-Hard: self-correction 66.7% vs debate 60.7% (p<0.001). Qwen GSM-Hard (n=1017): debate 58.8%, self-correction 61.0%, noise control 63.2%.
limits: Llama-3.1-8B differences not significant (p=0.155, 0.131). Debate did beat single shot on Qwen GSM-Hard (58.8 vs 25.6), so some gain is just extra sampling.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G9: matched-cost isolated retries beat peer exchange.

source: Bertalanic & Fortuna (2026) The Cost of Consensus: Isolated Self-Correction Prevails Over Unguided Homogeneous Multi-Agent Debate - conformity mechanics
finding: Three failure routes: majority adoption, peer reasoning breaking correct answers, and voting discarding a right answer that was in the pool.
numbers: Modal-answer adoption up to 85.5%; vulnerability rate (correct trajectories destroyed) up to 70.0% (Ministral GSM-Hard); oracle gap up to 32.3 points. Conformity near ceiling at 2 peers: 69.4% at 2 peers vs 73.4% at 9 (GSM-Hard), 77.2% vs 85.5% (MMLU-Hard). Consensus rate Qwen GSM-Hard: debate 83.5% vs self-correction 73.0%.
limits: Models of 7-8B only; behaviour model-dependent.
agent_relevance: Conformity saturates fast, so cutting the number of peers does not fix it. Remove peers.

source: Rajasekaran & Vasileiou (2026) A Quantitative Approach to Asch Conformity in Frontier LLMs
finding: Six frontier models all moved toward a distractor word when told other participants gave it. The push grew up to 5 participants and then flattened. A far-off word got no push.
numbers: Cloze sentences, 100 trials per cell, group sizes 1, 2, 5, 10, temperature 1. Shift for a plausible alternative: 22 points at n=1, 49 points at n=10; change under 3 points between n=5 and n=10. Semantically far distractor: under 2 points for every model.
limits: Fabricated consensus rather than real peers. Model names as printed in the paper. One task type.
agent_relevance: The push is largest when the other answer is already plausible to the model, which is the case for a sibling sample of the same model.

source: Rajasekaran & Vasileiou (2026) Asch conformity - per model
finding: Models differ a lot in size of the shift but not in direction.
numbers: At n=10 for one question type, gemini-3.8-flash shifted +73 points, gpt-6-sol +68, gpt-6-luna +36, claude-sonnet-5-5 +39, claude-opus-5-5 +33 and gemini-4-argon +42. Filler words chosen in only 583 of 197,976 counted trials.
limits: Values read from a heat-map text dump; treat as approximate.
agent_relevance: Stronger or more confident models are not immune; test any model before relying on its independence.

source: Kong, Lai, Piao, Evans (2026) Multi-LLM Systems Exhibit Robust Semantic Collapse
finding: Closed-loop interaction among LLMs converges in meaning over 200 to 1,000 rounds even while wording stays varied.
numbers: Three model instances per run. Cosine distance between the last 500 rounds and the first 10 rounds: 0.192 (SD 0.056). Plateau predicted from the first 50 rounds (MAE 0.060).
limits: Open-ended generation, not answer accuracy.
agent_relevance: Diversity lost by interaction is lost early and stays lost.

source: Kong, Lai, Piao, Evans (2026) Semantic Collapse - interventions
finding: Thirteen interventions (decoding, prompts, agent composition, activation steering, RL) did not reliably restore semantic diversity.
numbers: Intervention runs 200 rounds, 3 replicates each. Only a custom diversity-targeted RL gave any positive effect. Authors say collapse is not solely due to alignment or conformity.
limits: Tested on a specific simulation scaffold.
agent_relevance: Do not plan to repair diversity afterwards with temperature or persona prompts (also G4: no persona voters).

source: Liu, Xiong, Zhang, Tang (2026) Social Networks of LLM Agents (SNLA)
finding: Narrow attention makes LLM groups herd; effective sample size stays bounded however many agents there are. Wide context restores crowd wisdom.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, greedy, 5 seeds. HiddenBench: wide minus narrow attention +0.64 collective accuracy; Werewolf +0.61. Werewolf narrow accuracy 0.00 at n=6, 8, 10, 12, 16 vs wide 0.87, 0.83, 0.70, 0.63, 0.59.
limits: Operator-controlled variants with an injected confident-wrong hub. Same model for all agents.
agent_relevance: More copies do not add independent evidence once they read each other.

source: Liu, Xiong, Zhang, Tang (2026) SNLA - ablations and boundaries
finding: Herding needs some social power and replicates on Llama; it is weak or absent in debate and a cooperative game.
numbers: Testbed (Qwen2.5-3B, n=12, 8 seeds): collective error 5.5 with social power 0 vs about 42 for any power above 0. Llama-3.1-8B: narrow collapse to 0.02, equaliser +0.37, adversary-off control 0.55. Du et al. debate variant (n=8, 5 seeds): accuracy 0.30 to 0.37, gap +0.07 (weak). GovSim: survival 12 months in all conditions.
limits: Authors report the debate and GovSim results as boundaries and negative results.
agent_relevance: Herding is not universal; it appears when a confident wrong source is present. Isolation removes the risk.

source: Pokharel & Dantu (2026) Hidden Anchors in Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation
finding: Classical consensus models fail for LLMs. Each model has a hidden internal belief that pulls its opinion no matter what neighbours say; strength of this differs by model.
numbers: 90 runs (30 each) on Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen3-32B, gpt-oss-20b. Held-out R2 for the full anchor model 0.44 on Llama vs 0.05 for both baselines. At margin 0.10 Llama opinions escape the initial hull in 77% of runs; Qwen and gpt-oss in about 25% or fewer.
limits: Small model set; classification-style tasks; anchor recovered by fitting.
agent_relevance: A model's prior is a stable attractor; same-model copies share it, so peer info adds little independent information.

source: Yazici, Kayaalp, Taga, Sayed (2026) Opinion Consensus Formation Among Networked LLMs
finding: Networked LLM agents reach consensus and disagreement decays exponentially, but the end point ignores starting opinions and network centrality.
numbers: DeGroot RMSE vs observed final opinions: 0.32. 3-class accuracy of DeGroot 32% (chance 33%); binary 60% (chance 50%). Convergence rate follows the second-largest eigenvalue. Self-weights 80% and 60% set by prompt.
limits: Opinion scores from sentiment analysis; topics like Bitcoin sentiment.
agent_relevance: Group answer is set by model bias, not by diverse starting views, so the starting diversity is wasted.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd - Study 1
finding: Averaging 12 different LLMs matched a crowd of 925 human forecasters.
numbers: 31 binary questions. LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.850. Acquiescence: mean model forecast above 50% though outcomes were about even.
limits: Small question set; different model families, not copies.
agent_relevance: Independent, heterogeneous samples do aggregate well.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd - Study 2
finding: Showing the human median to a model improved its forecast, but less than a plain average of model and human.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 (p=0.003); Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 (p<0.001); accuracy gain 17-28%. Interval width narrowed (GPT-4 17.75 to 14.22). Updated forecasts worse than simple average: Brier 0.13 and 0.14 (p=0.011, p=0.001).
limits: One-way influence from an outside crowd, not from peers of the same model.
agent_relevance: If outside evidence is added, combine it by averaging in code rather than asking the model to absorb it.

source: Chuang et al. (2025) Probing LLM World Models: Enhancing Guesstimation with Wisdom of Crowds Decoding
finding: Median of many independently sampled reasoning paths beat greedy, majority-vote self-consistency and mean decoding on estimates. A human crowd replication was run.
numbers: 30 sampled paths, 10 LLMs, three datasets (MARBLES has 15 questions). LLaMA-3.1-8B MARBLES normalised error: median 0.81, majority 0.94, mean 4.80, greedy 2.80. LLaMA-2-7B: median 1.25 vs majority 88.44 vs mean 3704.85. GPT-4: 1.00 vs 1.07 vs 1.29 vs 1.04.
limits: Gain is small on the strongest model. Numeric tasks only. Samples still share one model's bias.
agent_relevance: Independent draws plus a robust aggregator is the safe crowd for one agent. This is a method already usable in an agent loop.

source: Douven (2026) Wisdom of LLM Crowds: Aggregation and Contamination in Language Model Ensembles
finding: Learned aggregation of 15 LLMs beat every single model. Weights followed error diversity, not individual skill.
numbers: 254 binary prediction-market questions. Weight vs diversity Spearman rho=+0.482; weight vs individual rank rho=-0.075. Two-model formula Brier 0.231 vs 0.265 for the 15-model mean (-12.9%, 203 items). Logistic regression cut Brier by 23%, MLP by 15.6%.
limits: Preprint; binary markets; contamination confound (see next line).
agent_relevance: Value of a crowd is decorrelated errors; copies of one model have little.

source: Douven (2026) Wisdom of LLM Crowds - contamination
finding: Apparent skill gap between cloud and local models was mostly training-data contamination.
numbers: Gap fell from 35.8% to 8.9% on the 94-item clean subset. About 26% of markets needed a fallback prior at the earliest cutoff.
limits: Small clean subset.
agent_relevance: Check for leakage before crediting any aggregation gain.

source: Fang, Wei, Chen (2026) Harnessing the Wisdom of LLM Crowds through Complementarity-Driven Iterative Collaboration (WILC)
finding: A gated relay: each next model is chosen to fix the previous output's bottleneck, and its change is accepted only if it improves the answer.
numbers: Four benchmarks; abstract claims performance comparable to GPT-5.2 at about 7x lower per-query cost. Dual gate: prospective complementarity fit and posterior complementarity gain.
limits: Only the abstract and framing were read; benchmark figures not extracted. Influence is sequential by design.
agent_relevance: A possible exception to isolation, but only if the acceptance gate is a real check and the gain is measured.

source: Sun et al. (2026) The Collaboration Tax: How Much LLM Multi-Agent Systems Pay to Coordinate
finding: Two LLMs with private views do worse than one alone; the tax falls as capability rises. The cause is a four-step chat cascade ending in accepting the partner's answer without re-deriving it.
numbers: 32 tasks, 11 models, 7 providers. In mixed pairs the tax moves toward the stronger partner. A prompt targeting all four stages closed part of the gap (share not extracted).
limits: Abstract and first page read only.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as conformity: accept nothing without re-derivation.

source: Rosenberg, Willcox, Schumann (2023) Towards Collective Superintelligence, a pilot study
finding: Structured real-time human chat linked by an LLM beat the survey crowd on a gumball estimate. Here social influence is used on purpose.
numbers: 241 participants. CSI group error within 12%; mean individual error 55%; survey crowd error 25%; GPT-4 alone 42% (p<0.001 vs individuals).
limits: Single task and run; vendor authors; no replication. Opposite to the Lorenz pattern, probably because small sub-groups deliberate.
agent_relevance: Counter-example for humans only; says nothing about copies of one model.
